opening.headline: When you have principles for responsible AI but don't know how to use them in the field, you learn how to translate the principles into tasks like defining, evaluating, mitigating, and disclosing.
body: Although companies have Responsible AI principles listed on their websites, they often don't have a space on their development calendars. Services for customers have a set release date, and inspection items vary from person to person. If principles remain abstract, they are ultimately left to the intuition of those in charge.

In this class, we will look at what axes Google's AI principles consist of and what tasks the Responsible Generative AI Toolkit translates the principles into. Next, we identify the four types of safety evaluations, academic benchmarks, model limitations and recommended procedures, and the implications of differential evaluation research on operational procedures, and explain the pre-launch inspection procedures for customer services as an example.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the composition of responsible AI principles and tools
Distinguish between bias and fairness assessment research and its implications for operational procedures

screens.title: I have principles, but I don't know how to use them in the field.
screens.lead: This scene shows the gap between the principle document and the development site. As you read, look for blank spaces.

paragraphs: The company's website features a statement of its Responsible AI principles. However, when I open the development schedule, there is no column corresponding to that principle anywhere. There are principles, but they are not reflected in schedules and outputs.

Customer-facing services have a set release date. Even if there is talk of doing maintenance right before launch, what to check varies from person to person. Some reps only check filters, while others only do legal reviews.

The more abstract the principle, the more it is ultimately left to the intuition of the person in charge. Inspections that rely on intuition have different results for each service, and it is difficult to explain what was missed after a problem occurs. It happens that two services created by the same team are released with different standards.
The questions for this class are: How to translate principles into concrete tasks such as policy definition, evaluation, mitigation, and disclosure.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: What more does it take to turn a statement of principles into a line on a release checklist? Answer this question again at the end of class. Think about who will be in charge, when, and what the output will be.

screens.outro: First, let me recall a similar experience. Move on to the next screen, thinking about what checks were made and what was left blank.

screens.title: Think of a similar situation
screens.lead: If you think about the question on your own first and then select it, the instructor will organize it for you. You will not enter or submit an answer.

items.prompt: Think about whether anything was checked for safety or fairness before launch.
items.answer: Even if there are inspection items, it is often not decided who checks them, when and by what standards. If there are items but no person in charge, timing, or output, the inspection becomes just a formality. If inspections are just a formality, they only place responsibility when a problem occurs and cannot prevent recurrence. This class covers how to turn the process into one that has those three things in place.

items.prompt: Have you ever thought that AI results could be unfavorable to certain groups?
items.answer: The model may reflect biases that were present in the training data. Even if the same question is marked differently for gender or origin, the results may vary. This difference is not noticeable in normal use, so it must be measured deliberately.

items.prompt: Have you ever seen a document or screen that informs users of the limitations of AI?
items.answer: Representative examples include model cards and service information. Knowing the limits allows users to decide how much to trust the results. Transparency is one of the key ways to translate principles into deliverables on the ground. One document can set your users' expectations straight.

screens.outro: Now let's take a look at what Google AI Principles consist of.

screens.title: The three pillars of Google AI Principles
screens.lead: Expand each item to see the three pillars of Google's AI Principles and what they mean. The last item summarizes why you need to turn principles into actions.

items.title: Axis 1. Bold Innovation
items.body: It's about developing AI that helps people feel supported and empowered in almost every field. It includes the principle of developing and deploying models and applications that significantly outweigh expected risks against predictable risks. This means not only avoiding risks, but also weighing benefits and risks. It is not a principle to stop a release just because there is even the slightest risk, but a principle to move forward while being aware of the risk and reducing it.

items.title: Axis 2: Responsible Development and Distribution
items.body: Based on the premise that AI is still a developing technology and its complexity and risks continue to change, it is an axis that takes responsibility for the entire life cycle from design to testing, deployment, and iteration. Have appropriate human oversight, due diligence and feedback mechanisms in place, and rigorous design, testing, monitoring and safeguards to reduce unintended harmful consequences and unfair biases. It also promotes respect for privacy, security, and intellectual property rights. This axis is the focus of this lesson, and each phrase becomes a candidate for inspection.

items.title: Axis 3: Making Progress Together
items.body: The axis is about collaborating with a variety of partners and helping others create their own solutions using AI. In this direction, Google releases tools and guidance for developers. An example is the Responsible Generative AI Toolkit in the following screen.

items.title: Why you need to turn principles into actions
items.body: Principles provide direction but are not checks in themselves. Phrases like supervising, testing, and monitoring people on the Responsible Development and Deployment axis become actionable only when organizations translate them into concrete tasks, personnel, and deliverables. The tools and procedures below will help you with that translation.

screens.outro: Let's take a look at the schematic diagram of a set of tools for translating principles into actions.

screens.title: Composition of Responsible Generative AI Toolkit
screens.lead: Selecting the numbered marker in the picture will display a description of what each of the four areas of the toolkit can help you with. Notice the flow that follows from justice to protection.

visual.alt: A four-step schematic of responsible application design, safety alignment, model evaluation, and safeguarding from left to right.
labels: Allowed/Prohibited Content, Risk Mitigation Approach, Model Card
Safety, fairness, reality evaluation, response comparison

markers.label: application design
markers.title: 1. Responsible application design
markers.body: First, system-level policies define what content is allowed and what content is prohibited. We then design approaches to reduce risk and communicate them transparently to users and stakeholders through documents such as model cards. For security risks unique to AI, refer to the risks and responses outlined by Google's SAIF.

markers.label: safety alignment
markers.title: 2. Safe alignment
markers.body: This step is to align the model's behavior with the defined safety policy. Debug prompts, make fine-tuning, and use RLHF (Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback) to adjust your model to respond to your policies.

markers.label: Model evaluation
markers.title: 3. Model evaluation
markers.body: Assess whether the model meets standards for safety, fairness, and realism. Use tools to compare model responses to each other. The four types of evaluation methods are discussed in detail in the following screen.

markers.label: safety device
markers.title: 4. Placement of safety devices
markers.body: Place safety sorters before and after service. You can use a pre-made classifier or create your own and deploy it. This is a final layer of protection in case your model isn't perfectly aligned.

markers.label: meaning of order
markers.title: The order of the four areas
markers.body: The sequence of define, align, evaluate, and protect is the basic flow that translates principles into action. Define what is acceptable, fit the model to it, evaluate whether it actually fits, and safeguard any remaining risks. When these four spaces are included in the development schedule, the principles are reflected in the schedule.

screens.outro: There is more than one area of assessment. Let’s compare the four types in a table.

screens.title: Assessment and Mitigation Phases: Four Types of Safety Assessments and Academic Benchmarks
screens.lead: Read the table from top to bottom to identify who, when and for what safety assessments are performed.

The levels of different models are compared against the same criteria. There are limitations in that results vary depending on implementation method and may differ from the actual distribution of questions in our service.
data.notes: Academic benchmarks cover things like toxicity, hate speech, factuality, and bias. Although useful when comparing different models, results vary depending on how they are implemented and have limitations. So, in addition to the benchmark, you need to create your own safety evaluation dataset suitable for your service. The four types do not replace each other and are deployed at different points in the life cycle. If you omit either type, you will miss a weakness that can only be found by that type. If your organization is small, external evaluations can be simplified by having them as regular checks. During development, we quickly check through development evaluation, create a basis for judgment through assurance evaluation at the end of major stages, and find weaknesses through red team and external evaluation in between.

screens.outro: To understand the limitations of an evaluation, you must also understand the limitations of the model itself. Confirm on the next screen. Because what the evaluation shows is only some of the model's limitations.

screens.title: Responsible AI Documentation Addresses Model Limitations and Recommended Procedures
screens.lead: When you hover over or select an underlined term in the text, an explanation appears. Discover the model's limitations and recommended procedures for adapting them.

data.text: Gemini Enterprise documentation honestly acknowledges the limitations of the model. In rare scenarios present in the training data, edge case may overestimate or misinterpret context. If information is not grounded in real-world data, hallucination may emerge, leading to incorrect content. Fairness analysis is currently limited to gender, race, ethnicity, and religion, with an emphasis on English-language data, as indicated by limits of scope. Due to potentially limited domain expertise, context involving individual rights may require Supervision by a meaningful person. If inputs or outputs exceed Token Limit, safety classifiers may not apply. The recommended procedure is to conduct a security risk assessment, perform safety testing tailored to use cases, set up safety filters, and then implement feedback and monitoring.

terms.tip: This is a rare situation in the training data. In these cases, the model may respond overly confidently or misunderstand the context.

This is false information that was made up to be plausible and not based on actual information. This can be reduced by providing supporting data. Another way is to instruct people to answer “don’t know” to unfounded questions.

This means that fairness analysis is limited to some axes and some languages. On axes that have not been analyzed, biases may still be undetected. If it is a Korean language service, you should evaluate it yourself rather than simply believing the analysis results that focus on English data. One way is to include questions in Korean and scenarios reflecting the Korean context in the evaluation set.
It is not a formal confirmation, but an oversight that people can actually judge and change. This is especially necessary in contexts that have significant implications for individual rights.
The amount of input and output the model can process at one time. If this limit is exceeded, the safety classifier may not be applied, so length restrictions must also be considered.

screens.outro: Now let's look at a specific example of fairness evaluation: discrimination evaluation research.

screens.title: Implications of differential evaluation research for operational procedures
screens.lead: Switch between two states to see what Anthropic's differential assessment study showed and what it means for your operating procedures.

states.label: What the Study Showed
states.body:
This research presents a way to proactively assess the differential impact of decisions made by language models, even for uses that have not yet been deployed. We use the model to create a wide range of prompts for decision makers across 70 different decision scenarios and systematically change the demographic information in each prompt.

In the absence of intervention, both positive and negative discrimination emerged in some settings. We showed that changing the prompt design can significantly reduce discrimination in the two directions.

However, the authors state that they do not endorse or allow automatic decision-making of language models in these high-risk applications. Saying that an evaluation method is good and using it for its intended purpose are two different things.

states.label: Implications for operating procedures
states.body:
First, we include **pairwise comparisons** in the evaluation procedure with only demographic variables changed. In the same scenario, just change information such as name, age, or gender to see if the results change. This can be done before release, even for uses that have not yet been deployed. The more scenarios you have, the more likely you are to discover differences that only appear in certain settings.

Second, if a difference is found, see if it can be reduced by prompt design, reduce it, and then measure again.

Third, we **document** the results and methods. You must leave a record of what scenarios were compared so that you can check them later during inspection and warranty evaluation.

Finally, closing the gap with prompts doesn't mean you can automatically make high-stakes decisions. The reduced gap is something we will continue to measure in the future, and will need to be revisited as the scenario changes.

screens.outro: Now that we've looked at all the principles, tools, and assessments, let's tie them all together into a pre-launch review process.

screens.title: Explanation: Inspection procedure before launching service to customers ① Definition and design
screens.lead: The instructor will explain the pre-launch inspection of the chatbot, which answers customer inquiries and provides information on refunds, across two screens. First, follow the definition and design steps step by step.

steps.title: Service introduction
steps.body: The service to be inspected is a chatbot that answers customer inquiries and provides guidance on whether refunds are possible. Among the three pillars of the principles, the goal is to move responsible development and deployment into the pre-release inspection process.

steps.title: Step 1. define policy
steps.body: Decide in sentences the topics on which the chatbot can answer, the content that should be prohibited, and the conditions under which it must be handed over to a human. For example, write that information on refund policy is allowed, but legal judgments or requests to confirm personal information are passed on to a counselor. A policy must be written as a sentence to provide a standard for subsequent evaluation.

steps.title: Step 2. Design safe access
steps.body: Establish filters, system guidelines, and human checkpoints. Just as increasing safety reduces ease of use, we also document trade-offs between technology and business. There must remain a basis for deciding which risks to accept and to what extent. For example, if refund decisions are confirmed by humans rather than chatbots, the speed will be slower, but the damage from errors will be reduced.

steps.title: Step 3. Ensure transparency
steps.body: Limitations of the service are written in documents such as model cards and user guidance. Users should be able to see that the chatbot is AI, that answers may be wrong, and how to connect to human advice. Hiding limitations causes users to become overconfident in their results.

steps.title: Correspondence to principles
steps.body: Indicate how the three steps correspond to items in the principle. Policy definition corresponds to human supervision, safe access design corresponds to rigorous design and inspection, and transparency corresponds to a feedback system. This correspondence table serves as evidence that the principles are reflected in the schedule. Even after the inspection is over, the same ticket can be reused for the next service.

screens.outro: Next, we move on to the evaluation, protection, and monitoring steps.

screens.title: Explanation: Pre-launch inspection procedure ② Evaluation, protection, monitoring
screens.lead: The instructor will explain the remaining steps to actually check the policy defined in the previous screen. Skip the steps with the arrows.

steps.title: Step 4. Evaluate development
steps.body: We evaluate the development by pairwise comparison of fairness with the adversarial query dataset for self-service. Simply change the customer's name or origin information in the refund information to see if the results change. Public benchmarks alone do not tell us the risks of this service. The questions and results used in the evaluation are stored so that they can be reused in the assurance evaluation.

steps.title: Step 5. Receive a warranty evaluation
steps.body: Reviewers outside the development team view the evaluation results against release criteria. It's easy for developers to miss weaknesses in their own designs, so an outside perspective is needed. The results of the assurance evaluation are used as basis for the meeting to decide whether to release the product. If standards are not met at this stage, the launch is delayed or its scope is reduced.

steps.title: Step 6. Decide on safety devices
steps.body: Set thresholds for safety classifiers and filters, and consider length limits for inputs and outputs. This is because the classifier may not be applied on inputs that exceed the token limit. Set up rules to reject or split very long input.

steps.title: Step 7. Continues after launch
steps.body: We receive user feedback and continue to monitor content. Issues found after release are added back to the evaluation dataset and reflected in the next release. This way, the evaluation dataset becomes increasingly sophisticated, capturing actual experiences of the service.

steps.title: Output becomes an inspection record
steps.body: When the outputs of each stage, namely policy documents, evaluation results, assurance review opinions, safeguard settings, and monitoring records, are accumulated, they become responsible AI inspection records. This is a way to leave principles as evidence rather than just saying them. Having a record will allow you to repeat the same checks more quickly on the next release. Even if the person in charge changes, the level of inspection is maintained.

screens.outro: Finally, we organize the entire class.

screens.title: Key points and reflection
screens.lead: The flow from principles to inspection procedures is organized into one.

paragraphs: The Google AI Principles are built around three pillars: Bold Innovation, Responsible Development and Deployment, and Progress Together. Since the principles themselves are not checkpoints, the work moves to the order of definition, alignment, evaluation, and protection suggested by the Responsible Generative AI Toolkit.

Safety assessments place development assessments, assurance assessments, red teams, and external assessments into the life cycle. Academic benchmarks are useful for comparison, but they have limitations and require self-serving datasets. Differential assessment studies show how to proactively measure the problem with pairwise comparisons that only change demographics, along with a cautious approach to not endorsing high-stakes automated decisions.

The answer to the initial question, what does it take to turn a statement of principle into a line on a checklist, is who is in charge, when, and what is delivered. Principles without these three remain mere slogans. Even after launch, we continue to provide feedback and monitoring and update inspection records. Maintenance is not an event that ends on launch date; it is an ongoing activity while the service is in operation.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Think about where the empty inspection stage is in your service launch process, and what the person in charge and output of that stage will be.

glossary.def: Google's AI principles center on bold innovation, responsible development and deployment, and making progress together.
A collection of tools and guidelines to assist with application design, safety alignment, model evaluation, and safeguarding.
An evaluation performed for governance purposes on a standard dataset by a group outside the development team.
This is an evaluation that measures differences in model decisions by varying demographic information.
This is a transparency document that communicates the purpose and limitations of the model.

misconceptions.fact: To be implemented, the principles must be translated into the work of policy definition, evaluation, mitigation, and disclosure. Inspection requires a person in charge, timing, and output.

misconceptions.myth: Just passing the public benchmark is enough.
misconceptions.fact: Benchmarks have different results and limitations depending on how they are implemented. You must create an evaluation dataset suitable for your service.

misconceptions.myth: Since discrimination is reduced with prompts, it can be used for automatic decisions.
misconceptions.fact: The study authors also state that they do not approve or disapprove of the model's automatic decisions in high-risk applications. There is a difference between something that has decreased and something that has disappeared.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: The principles translate into tasks of policy definition, evaluation, mitigation, and disclosure.
Evaluation is divided into development, assurance, red team, and external evaluation and placed in the life cycle.
Discrimination assessments are measured a priori by pairwise comparisons where only demographics are changed.
We will continue to provide feedback and monitoring even after launch.
